counterexample: Base-case failure at 0024: G on {u,w,v} with edges u->v, u->w, w->v. The shortest u->v path has length 1, yet w is an intermediate vertex with (u,w),(w,v) in GT, so (u,v) is NOT in R, contradicting the base case's claim. Independently, the converse direction is false at k=2: G = {v1->v2, v2->v1} is cyclic but its transitive closure GT = {(v1,v1),(v1,v2),(v2,v1),(v2,v2)} forces any graph with closure GT to contain both edges (only 2 vertices are available, so v1 must reach v2 and v2 must reach v1 by direct edges), so the 2-edge set {(v1,v2),(v2,v1)} is the unique transitive reduction. Similarly a single vertex with a self-loop is cyclic with a unique reduction. So the theorem as stated is false and no repair of lines 0047-0058 can rescue it.
reasoning_summary: 0001 Header, no content to check. 0002-0007 Verbatim restatement of the problem's definitions (transitive closure GT, transitive reduction as a minimum-edge graph whose closure is GT); accurate copy, nothing to verify. 0008 Theorem statement matches the problem. 0009 Continuation of the theorem statement; fine. 0010 Announces proof of both directions; acceptable plan. 0011 Labels the direction 'G acyclic => unique reduction' (the arrow label is inverted relative to the biconditional's usual reading, but the content is a genuine half of the equivalence); harmless. 0012 'G acyclic => GT acyclic': correct, since a cycle in GT would concatenate to a closed walk, hence a cycle, in G. 0013 Parenthetical justification is terse but correct. 0014 Introduces the candidate reduction R; fine. 0015 Definition R = {(u,v) in GT : no w != u,v with (u,w),(w,v) in GT} is well formed. 0016 Equation tag only. 0017-0018 Informal gloss of R (edges not obtainable by composing two GT edges); consistent with 0015. 0019 Lemma 1 statement (R^T = GT); a legitimate goal. 0020 'R subset of GT implies R^T subset of GT': correct because GT is transitive, so it is closed under composition. 0021-0022 Announces strong induction on the length of the SHORTEST path from u to v; the choice of induction measure is the source of the failure below (longest-path length is the measure that works in a DAG). 0023 'shortest path of length 1 means (u,v) is an edge of G, hence of GT': correct. 0024 FIRST FAILING STEP. Asserts that when the shortest u->v path has length 1 there is no intermediate w with u->w->v, hence (u,v) is in R. This is false: a direct edge can coexist with a longer route, e.g. edges u->v, u->w, w->v give shortest length 1 while w witnesses (u,w),(w,v) in GT, so (u,v) is excluded from R by 0015. The base case therefore does not establish (u,v) in R. 0025 'thus (u,v) in R^T' inherits the invalid premise of 0024 and is unjustified. 0026 Inductive step setup (shortest path length k>1; if (u,v) in R we are done) is fine. 0027 'Otherwise there exists w != u,v with (u,w),(w,v) in GT' is justified: it is the negation of the defining condition in 0015. 0028 SECOND, INDEPENDENT FAILURE. Claims the shortest u->w and w->v distances are strictly less than k 'since G is acyclic'. Acyclicity gives only dist(u,w)+dist(w,v) >= k; a witness w may lie only on a long detour, e.g. u->x->v (k=2) together with u->a->b->w and w->v, where dist(u,w)=3 > k. Since 0027 supplies an arbitrary witness w, the measure need not decrease. 0029 The appeal to the inductive hypothesis is therefore unsupported; the closing 'by transitivity' (R^T transitive) would be fine if the hypothesis applied. Lemma 1 is a true statement for DAGs, but this proof of it is broken at 0024 and 0028. 0030-0031 Lemma 2 statement (R is edge-minimal) is a legitimate goal. 0032 Setup: take any R' with R'^T = GT and show |R'| >= |R|; fine. 0033 Restates the defining property of (u,v) in R; correct. 0034 'any path from u to v in GT must include the direct edge (u,v)' is loosely phrased (the relevant graph is R', not GT) but the intended content is used correctly below. 0035 R'^T = GT gives a u->v path in R'; correct. 0036 If (u,v) is not in R', that path has length >= 2 and passes through an intermediate w' with (u,w'),(w',v) in R'^T; correct, and w' != u,v holds because R'^T = GT is acyclic (0012) so the path is simple — the proof leaves this sub-point implicit, a minor gap only. 0037 Transfers (u,w'),(w',v) to GT and contradicts membership of (u,v) in R; valid. 0038 Concludes R subset of R', hence |R'| >= |R|; valid. 0039 Lemma 3 statement (uniqueness) is the right goal. 0040-0041 Page-break artifacts, no content. 0042 'R is a transitive reduction' follows from Lemmas 1 and 2 (conditional on the broken proof of Lemma 1). 0043-0044 Takes another reduction R' with |R'| = |R| and R'^T = GT; fine. 0045 Uses the containment R subset of R' extracted from Lemma 2's proof plus equal cardinality to get R = R'; valid reasoning. 0046 States the contrapositive form of the second direction ('not acyclic => multiple reductions'); a legitimate strategy. 0047 Fixes a simple cycle C = (v1,...,vk,v1) with k >= 2; incomplete, since a self-loop (k=1) also makes G cyclic and is never handled — and a lone self-loop has a unique reduction, so the omitted case is not benign. 0048-0049 '(vi,vj) in GT for all i != j' is correct for vertices of a cycle. 0050 Announces two candidate edge sets; fine. 0051-0052 R1 = the original k-cycle edges together with E'; well defined. 0053-0054 FAILS: R2 = {(v1,v3),(v3,v4),...,(vk,v2),(v2,v1)} is ill defined when k = 2 (no vertex v3), so the promised second reduction does not exist in the k=2 case, which line 0047 explicitly admits. This is fatal rather than cosmetic: for a 2-cycle both edges are forced, so the reduction really is unique and the claimed conclusion is false. 0055-0056 E' is described only as 'a transitive reduction of G restricted to vertices outside C (with appropriate connections maintained)' — an unjustified hand-wave that never verifies that one and the same E' yields closure GT alongside both R1 and R2. 0057-0058 Describes R2 as a different Hamiltonian cycle on C; correct only for k >= 3, vacuous/false at k = 2. 0059 'k edges is minimal, fewer would disconnect the cycle' is asserted without proof, and global minimality of R1 and R2 over the whole vertex set is never established, so neither is shown to be a transitive reduction. 0060-0063 The claim (R1)^T|C = (R2)^T|C = complete digraph on C is correct for k >= 3, but the inference that the full closures equal GT depends on the unverified E' of 0055-0056. 0064-0065 'R1 != R2 hence non-uniqueness' presupposes both are genuine (minimum) reductions, which 0059 did not establish, and the exhibited distinguishing edges (v1,v2),(v1,v3) again require k >= 3. 0066 Page number; no content. Overall: the proof fails first at 0024 (and again at 0028) in the acyclic direction, and the converse direction is unsound at 0047/0053 where the omitted k<=2 cases are in fact counterexamples to the theorem as stated.
